name: Night Tank
description: Fictional thermal-storage seed pitch with modeled site economics.

slides.title: NIGHT TANK
items: Cooling storage for commercial buildings
Illustrative seed pitch

slides.title: The expensive hour is short
items: A building can pay for a peak it reaches only briefly. Our first customer is a facilities director with chilled-water cooling, an afternoon demand charge and spare chiller capacity overnight.
Charge overnight
Discharge at peak
In this example the tank charges before 07:00 and supplies cooling from 14:00 to 18:00. The chiller handles the rest of the day.

slides.title: Cold goes into the tank at night
items: An existing chiller freezes water around a submerged coil. During the peak window, the building loop draws cooling from the tank as the ice melts.
A bypass allows the operator to isolate storage and return to normal chiller operation. The retrofit starts with a site survey of valves, available space and overnight load.

slides.title: The peak falls by 80 kW
items: Illustrative site model • electrical load in kW
At 16:00, modeled chiller draw drops from 240 to 160 kW. Night charging adds load earlier. The tariff and the timing of the monthly peak determine the actual saving.

slides.title: One contract per plant
items: $900 / month
The owner buys the installed equipment separately. The subscription covers forecasting, dispatch and monthly reporting. Mechanical contractors earn installation and service revenue.
At an assumed $22 per kW per month, an 80 kW reduction is worth $1,760 in gross monthly demand savings. After our fee, $860 remains before energy costs, financing and maintenance.

slides.title: Start with 300 plants
items: Annual subscription opportunity in the initial territory if all 300 qualified sites adopt at $10,800 per year. This is a planning scenario.
Screen for a central loop, sufficient tank space and a rate schedule with a meaningful demand charge. Remove sites that fail any one of those tests.

slides.title: Sell through the plant room
items: A contractor brings a year of interval data to the first meeting. We model the peak, then price a paid survey if the customer’s tariff supports the case.
The first installation includes a metered baseline and an agreed comparison period. The owner sees both peak reduction and overnight electricity use before signing a portfolio rollout.

slides.title: A pilot with an exit test
items: Baseline
Four weeks of meter and weather data establish a comparison for similar operating days.
Dispatch
The operator can override dispatch. Every override and the reason for it appear in the site log.
Decision
Advance only if peak reduction exceeds 60 kW on ten eligible days and occupied rooms stay within the owner’s agreed temperature range.

slides.title: Where storage earns its space
items: Load scheduling
Useful where the operator can shift the activity itself. A hotel still needs occupied rooms cooled through check-in.
Battery storage
Serves many electrical loads. Our proposal targets a narrower cooling job and requires an accessible chilled-water plant.
The deciding test
Compare installed cost and annual net savings for all three options using the same site data. A poor payback ends our sales process.

slides.title: Who commissions the system?
items: Thermal engineering
Lea Moreno owns sizing, coil design and acceptance testing. Her first hire is a commissioning engineer to shorten the time between survey and sign-off.
Controls and delivery
Sam Iqbal owns dispatch software and contractor training. Each installation leaves a local operator with a tested bypass and a documented handover.

slides.title: Eighteen months to six sites
items: Months 1–6
Commission two pilots and verify the meter baseline with each owner.
Months 7–12
Build the installation kit. Train two contractor crews and complete the third and fourth sites.
Months 13–18
Commission the last two sites. Seek renewals from the first cohort with a full season of billing evidence.

slides.title: Fund the first cooling season
items: $2.4M seed
$1.2M for equipment and commissioning, $720k for controls and measurement, and $480k for contractor support and sales.
The round targets six metered installations and two renewal decisions within 18 months. All venture details and figures in this pitch are fictional.
